label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
rationale: Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and no president under 40 percent approval has gained. Democrats need a net 3 from a 215 baseline. Redistricting nets Republicans roughly 4 to 10 seats. The median district sits about 3.4 points right of the nation (Sabato via Washington Examiner). So Democrats need a national House margin above roughly D+3.5. Markets put the median near D+8.5 to D+9. DDHQ (77) is stale by two days and weights fundamentals. Markets (90) are closer to the polling. Independence signal at lock: the Republican House super PAC abandoned two of its own incumbents three weeks out. Moved 88 to 90, the stated ceiling.
biggest_unknown: The final week's likely-voter generic ballot. Below D+4 makes this a toss-up.
counter_case: Polling error that overstates Democrats by 4 or more points, as in 2014, plus a map that converts a D+4 popular vote into fewer than 218 seats. Republicans hold the House in that world.
alternate: Republicans hold the House with 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: National House popular vote margin under D+3.5 on the certified count, or a final-week LV generic ballot average under D+4 with DCCC cuts in Trump +5 to +10 seats.
indep_signal: Committee triage. CLF canceled all remaining reservations for two GOP incumbents (IA-01, NJ-07) Oct 10-11, the first incumbent cuts of the cycle, and pulled money from MI-08, OH-01 and NE-02

label: House seats
question: House seats won by Democrats (of 435)
rationale: A D+8 national environment in 2018 produced 235 Democratic seats on a map 4.3 points right of the nation. The 2026 median seat is 3.4 points right. Fewer swing seats now flatten the curve. DDHQ says 235. Kalshi brackets imply 235 with an 80 percent range of 219 to 250. We sit slightly lower and wider at the bottom for polling error. Independence signal at lock: CLF cancellations. Moved 234 to 235.
biggest_unknown: Whether the Texas and Florida Hispanic-heavy seats swing back toward Democrats after 2024.
indep_signal: Committee triage. same CLF cancellations and reallocation
polymarket_missing: no polymarket market mapped to this item

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
rationale: Democrats need 51 (50 plus Vance is Republican). They hold 47 with caucusing independents and must net 4. Summing our race numbers gives an expected 50.5 Democratic seats. With correlated outcomes that is close to a coin flip. DDHQ says 56. Markets say 62 to 65. The gap is our shading of red-state polls (TX, OH, AK, IA). Red-state Senate polls overstated Democrats in the 2014 and 2018 midterms and in 2020 and 2024. Markets follow those polls. We shade toward the Republican. Independence signals at lock nudged NC, GA, SC and KS. Moved 52 to 53.
biggest_unknown: Whether the Texas and Ohio polls are right this time. Those two seats decide control in most paths.
counter_case: Midterms without Trump on the ballot have not shown the presidential-year pattern of Democratic poll overstatement. In 2022 polls underrated Democrats. If that holds, markets are right and control is near 65.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with TX or OH plus AK.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter polls in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state.
indep_signal: Committee triage. combined effect of the NC, GA, SC and KS signals above on the expected seat count (about +0.1 seats)

label: Senate seats
question: Senate seats held by Democrats plus independents who caucus with them, after the election (of 100)
rationale: Expected value from our race probabilities is 50.5. The 80 percent range covers losing MI and NH on the low side and sweeping ME, OH, TX and AK on the high side. Kalshi brackets imply 51.5 with 47 to 53.
biggest_unknown: Michigan. It is the only Democratic-held seat our numbers put below 80 percent.

label: House popular vote
question: National House popular vote, Democratic minus Republican, in points
ddhq_missing: DDHQ publishes no number for this item
rationale: Markets imply a median of D+8.5 (Polymarket) to D+9.2 (Kalshi). The Silver tracker was reported at D+8.9 on Oct 7 (search summary, not fetched). Midterm generic-ballot error has run both ways (2018 understated D by 1.3, 2014 understated R by 3.3). We take a half point off the market median for that asymmetry and keep the interval wide.

label: Senate · ME
question: Democrat wins the ME US Senate race
rationale: Harris won Maine by 6.9. Collins has beaten her polls in every race since 2008, by about 9 points in 2020. No fall poll was found. Jackson replaced Platner late. DDHQ 54, markets 57 to 60. We stay near DDHQ because Collins's personal vote is the strongest base rate in the race.
biggest_unknown: An independent fall poll. None was retrieved.

label: Senate · NC
question: Democrat wins the NC US Senate race
rationale: Open R seat. Trump won NC by 3.2. Cooper leads 54 to 40 (SurveyUSA, LV, Oct 7 to 11, fetched) and 50 to 43 (ECU, summary). DDHQ 84, markets 95 to 96. Cooper has won statewide six times. We sit between, closer to markets. Independence signal at lock: Republican outside groups have stopped spending here and the Democratic super PAC paused because Cooper is favored. Moved 92 to 95.
biggest_unknown: Whether the NC board's unsealed-envelope rule disqualifies ballots at scale. It cannot flip a 7-point race.
indep_signal: Committee triage. SLF paused all NC Senate spending Oct 2 after >$30M. GOP groups cut ~$15M of October bookings. Senate Majority PAC paused NC Oct 14 (Semafor, AdImpact via independence agent)

label: Senate · OH special
question: Democrat wins the OH US Senate race (special)
rationale: Special election. Trump won Ohio by 11.2. Brown leads by 6 (CNN) and 4 (YouGov), both from summaries. Ohio polls overstated Democrats by 4 to 6 points in 2022 and 2024, and Brown lost in 2024 after leading in polls. DDHQ 51, markets 65. Red-state Senate polls overstated Democrats in the 2014 and 2018 midterms and in 2020 and 2024. Markets follow those polls. We shade toward the Republican.
biggest_unknown: Whether Ohio polls carry the same Democratic bias in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.

label: Senate · TX
question: Democrat wins the TX US Senate race
rationale: Trump won Texas by 13.7. No Democrat has won statewide since 1994. One poll (TSU, LV, Sept 15 to 19) has Talarico up 1. Paxton is a weak nominee. A D+8 national swing plus a candidate-quality penalty gets the race to even. DDHQ 56, markets 62. Red-state Senate polls overstated Democrats in the 2014 and 2018 midterms and in 2020 and 2024. Markets follow those polls. We shade toward the Republican.
biggest_unknown: Hispanic turnout and vote share in South and West Texas versus 2024.

label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
rationale: Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and no president under 40 percent approval has gained. Democrats need a net 3 from a 215 baseline. Redistricting nets Republicans roughly 4 to 10 seats. The median district sits about 3.4 points right of the nation (Sabato via Washington Examiner). So Democrats need a national House margin above roughly D+3.5. Markets put the median near D+8.5 to D+9. DDHQ (77) is stale by two days and weights fundamentals. Markets (90) are closer to the polling. Independence signal at lock: the Republican House super PAC abandoned two of its own incumbents three weeks out. Moved 88 to 90, the stated ceiling.
biggest_unknown: The final week's likely-voter generic ballot. Below D+4 makes this a toss-up.
counter_case: Polling error that overstates Democrats by 4 or more points, as in 2014, plus a map that converts a D+4 popular vote into fewer than 218 seats. Republicans hold the House in that world.
alternate: Republicans hold the House with 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: National House popular vote margin under D+3.5 on the certified count, or a final-week LV generic ballot average under D+4 with DCCC cuts in Trump +5 to +10 seats.
indep_signal: Committee triage. CLF canceled all remaining reservations for two GOP incumbents (IA-01, NJ-07) Oct 10-11, the first incumbent cuts of the cycle, and pulled money from MI-08, OH-01 and NE-02

indep_signal: Committee triage. same CLF cancellations and reallocation

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
rationale: Democrats need 51 (50 plus Vance is Republican). They hold 47 with caucusing independents and must net 4. Summing our race numbers gives an expected 50.5 Democratic seats. With correlated outcomes that is close to a coin flip. DDHQ says 56. Markets say 62 to 65. The gap is our shading of red-state polls (TX, OH, AK, IA). Red-state Senate polls overstated Democrats in the 2014 and 2018 midterms and in 2020 and 2024. Markets follow those polls. We shade toward the Republican. Independence signals at lock nudged NC, GA, SC and KS. Moved 52 to 53.
biggest_unknown: Whether the Texas and Ohio polls are right this time. Those two seats decide control in most paths.
counter_case: Midterms without Trump on the ballot have not shown the presidential-year pattern of Democratic poll overstatement. In 2022 polls underrated Democrats. If that holds, markets are right and control is near 65.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with TX or OH plus AK.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter polls in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state.
indep_signal: Committee triage. combined effect of the NC, GA, SC and KS signals above on the expected seat count (about +0.1 seats)

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
weakest_component: Seat-vote conversion under the new maps.
confidence_ceiling: 0.90. Above that requires certainty the polls do not overstate Democrats, which history does not support.
rationale: Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946. Democrats need a net 3. Redistricting moved 4 to 10 seats right and the median seat sits about 3.4 points right of the nation, so Democrats need roughly D+3.5 nationally. Silver Bulletin's generic ballot is D+8.9 (Oct 20, retrieved) and Trump net approval is -22.3 (Silver, Oct 20, retrieved). Kalshi seat brackets imply 235 (retrieved). Markets 90.5 to 91.5, DDHQ 77 on a model still dated Oct 14. Nothing since the lock changes the cushion. Re-derived at 90, the ceiling.
biggest_unknown: The final-week likely-voter generic ballot. Below D+4 makes this a toss-up.
counter_case: A 2014-size polling miss of 4 or more points toward Republicans plus a map that turns D+4 into fewer than 218 seats.
alternate: Republicans hold the House with 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: Final-week LV generic ballot average under D+4 with DCCC or House Majority PAC cuts in Trump +5 to +10 seats.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate · OH special
question: Democrat wins the OH US Senate race (special)
rationale: Re-derived. Special election. Trump won Ohio by 11.2. Uniform swing from 2024 to a D+9 national environment puts a generic Democrat near even. Brown's personal vote and an appointed opponent add 2 to 3 points. Polls: 270toWin average Brown 47.6 Husted 44.6 (5 polls), CNN Brown +6, Siena +3, InsiderAdvantage +1, Suffolk +3 (retrieved). biggest_unknown: Whether Ohio polls carry their usual Republican miss with no Trump on the ballot.

biggest_unknown: Hispanic turnout and vote share in South and West Texas against 2024.

label: Senate · SC
question: Democrat wins the SC US Senate race
weakest_component: How much of 2020's 6.5-point polling miss to carry into a midterm: one cycle of evidence.
rationale: Base rate: no Democrat has won a South Carolina Senate race since 1998, and every race since has gone Republican by about 10 or more. Trump won the state by 17.9 in 2024. The national environment near D+8.1 among likely voters is worth about 9.6 points of swing from 2024, so the baseline lands near R+8.3. Darline Graham was appointed on July 13 after Lindsey Graham died, so she carries no long incumbency, and the model's rule treats appointees as open seats. Three nonpartisan likely-voter polls landed in four days: NYT/Siena tied at 48, The Citadel Graham +4 (Andrews +5 among registered voters), Targoz Graham +1. Their average is about Graham +1.7, and the partisan polls sit in the same band, Graham +4 to Andrews +1. In 2020 the state's final polling average had the Republican up 3.7 and the result was Republican +10.2, a 6.5-point miss toward the Democrat, one cycle with Trump on the ballot. Carrying half of that miss puts the polls near Graham +5, and the baseline pulls about a point further, to Graham +6. The early electorate looks like 2022's: the counties Harris won are 24.3 percent of ballots against 24.8 at the same point in 2022, the three metro counties 28.0 against 27.3, the Black share of mail ballots 26.8 against 24.2 at 2022's close. Markets near 26, Decision Desk 30, nine of ten raters Lean R. Andrews at 14 percent, up from 5.
biggest_unknown: Whether this year's South Carolina polls miss toward the Democrat as 2020's did, in a midterm without Trump on the ballot.
counter_case: The three polls are right. South Carolina's 2020 miss came with Trump on the ballot and low-propensity Republicans turning out for him, and a midterm with an appointed Republican and a D+8 environment does not repeat it. Then the race is about Graham +2 and Andrews near 35 percent.
alternate: Polls right: Graham by about 2 (80 percent Graham +8 to Andrews +4), Andrews near 35 percent.
flip_trigger: A nonpartisan likely-voter poll with Andrews ahead, or the county early-vote file showing the Harris counties' share at or above 2022's same point by the close of early voting on Oct 31.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
weakest_component: The seat count under the new maps. No district polling exists in most redrawn seats, so the raters' calls are the only read.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and every midterm since 1994 with the president under 45 percent approval flipped the House when the other party did not already hold it. Trump is at 37.8 approve, 59.8 disapprove across 16 polls since Oct 20 (retrieved). Democrats hold 214 and need 218. The nonpartisan generic ballot averages D+8.1 over 28 polls since Oct 20, D+7.9 among likely voters (retrieved). The chamber model, which reads the raters' ratings for every House seat and shares one 3-point national swing, puts the chance at 81 with a mean of 231 seats (retrieved from scripts/chambers.py). Markets price 93 to 94.5. The model's width comes from its national swing and the ratings' coarseness, and the historical record argues for more than 81. The markets ignore the live downside: a 3-to-4-point poll miss toward Republicans, which I put near 30 percent, still clears 218 most of the time at D+4.5, but not always. Redistricting moved 16 seats toward Republicans and the raters already have 5 of them flipping. 88.
biggest_unknown: The size and direction of the generic-ballot miss. The record since 1994 is 1 to 4 points with no fixed direction in a midterm.
counter_case: The polls overstate Democrats by 5 or more, as in 1980 and 1948 nationally and never yet in a midterm, and the new maps are worth more than the raters show. Then the vote lands near D+3 and Republicans keep 218 to 222.
alternate: Republicans hold the House at 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: Before the election: a final likely-voter generic average under D+5. On the night: Democrats failing to flip PA-07, PA-08 and NY-17 by 11 pm ET, or a Republican lead in the national House vote with the East Coast counted.

label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
weakest_component: The seat count under the new maps. No district polling exists in most redrawn seats, so the raters' calls are the only read.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and every midterm since 1994 with the president under 45 percent approval flipped the House when the other party did not already hold it. Trump is at 37.8 approve, 59.8 disapprove across 16 polls since Oct 20 (retrieved). Democrats hold 214 and need 218. The nonpartisan generic ballot averages D+8.1 over 28 polls since Oct 20, D+7.9 among likely voters (retrieved). The chamber model, which reads the raters' ratings for every House seat and shares one 3-point national swing, puts the chance at 81 with a mean of 231 seats (retrieved from scripts/chambers.py). Markets price 93 to 94.5. The model's width comes from its national swing and the ratings' coarseness, and the historical record argues for more than 81. The markets ignore the live downside: a 3-to-4-point poll miss toward Republicans, which I put near 30 percent, still clears 218 most of the time at D+4.5, but not always. Redistricting moved 16 seats toward Republicans and the raters already have 5 of them flipping. 88.
biggest_unknown: The size and direction of the generic-ballot miss. The record since 1994 is 1 to 4 points with no fixed direction in a midterm.
counter_case: The polls overstate Democrats by 5 or more, as in 1980 and 1948 nationally and never yet in a midterm, and the new maps are worth more than the raters show. Then the vote lands near D+3 and Republicans keep 218 to 222.
alternate: Republicans hold the House at 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: Before the election: a final likely-voter generic average under D+5. On the night: Democrats failing to flip PA-07, PA-08 and NY-17 by 11 pm ET, or a Republican lead in the national House vote with the East Coast counted.

The pickups run through Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Alaska, states Trump won by 11 to 14 where Senate polls overstated Democrats in 2018, 2022 and 2024 by 3 to 5 points, and I take that history at about two thirds of its face value. counter_case: The 2025 pattern holds: polls are right or understate Democrats, Brown and Talarico win by 4 or more, Jackson and Peltola win, and Democrats reach 52 or 53. Under that case the right number tonight is 75 or higher.
alternate: Republicans hold the Senate at 50 or 51 seats: Democrats take North Carolina and Maine, lose Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Kansas, and hold Michigan narrowly or not at all.
flip_trigger: On the night: Ohio called for Husted, or Brown trailing with 80 percent counted; Ossoff under +5 when Georgia reports around 9 pm ET; Rogers ahead in Michigan with Wayne County mostly in. Any one of these moves the primary to the alternate.

rationale: Re-derived from zero. Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and every midterm since 1994 with the president under 45 percent approval flipped the House when the other party did not already hold it. Trump is at 37.8 approve, 59.8 disapprove across 16 polls since Oct 20 (retrieved). Democrats hold 214 and need 218. The nonpartisan generic ballot averages D+8.1 over 28 polls since Oct 20, D+7.9 among likely voters (retrieved). The chamber model, which reads the raters' ratings for every House seat and shares one 3-point national swing, puts the chance at 81 with a mean of 231 seats (retrieved from scripts/chambers.py). Markets price 93 to 94.5. The model's width comes from its national swing and the ratings' coarseness, and the historical record argues for more than 81. The markets ignore the live downside: a 3-to-4-point poll miss toward Republicans, which I put near 30 percent, still clears 218 most of the time at D+4.5, but not always. Redistricting moved 16 seats toward Republicans and the raters already have 5 of them flipping. 88.
biggest_unknown: The size and direction of the generic-ballot miss. The record since 1994 is 1 to 4 points with no fixed direction in a midterm.
counter_case: The polls overstate Democrats by 5 or more, as in 1980 and 1948 nationally and never yet in a midterm, and the new maps are worth more than the raters show. Then the vote lands near D+3 and Republicans keep 218 to 222.
alternate: Republicans hold the House at 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: Before the election: a final likely-voter generic average under D+5. On the night: Democrats failing to flip PA-07, PA-08 and NY-17 by 11 pm ET, or a Republican lead in the national House vote with the East Coast counted.

weakest_component: Alaska, where the whole read rests on one nonpartisan poll, two Republican-sponsored polls that also show Peltola ahead, and her statewide history. Then Maine, where seven polls say one thing and one candidate's 2020 record says another.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats hold 47 with the two independents and need 51, a net gain of 4 from nine Republican-held races in play. Summing this run's race numbers gives 50.8 expected Democratic seats: pickups worth 4.2 (NC 0.96, ME 0.70, OH 0.58, AK 0.55, TX 0.52, KS 0.40, IA 0.34, SC 0.12, FL 0.06) against losses worth 0.5 (MI 0.30, MN 0.07, NH 0.06, GA 0.04). The core model says 70.5 and the markets 71.5 (retrieved); both read the state polls at face value. The pickups run through Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Alaska, states Trump won by 11 to 14 where Senate polls overstated Democrats in 2018, 2022 and 2024 by 3 to 5 points, and I take that history at about two thirds of its face value. The lock said 53 and the Oct 28 run 55; this number is re-derived, not carried.
biggest_unknown: Whether the Ohio and Texas polls miss toward Republicans again, as in 2022 and 2024, or toward Democrats, as Virginia and New Jersey did in 2025. Nothing before Tuesday night settles it.
counter_case: The 2025 pattern holds: polls are right or understate Democrats, Brown and Talarico win by 4 or more, Jackson and Peltola win, and Democrats reach 52 or 53. Under that case the right number tonight is 75 or higher.
alternate: Republicans hold the Senate at 50 or 51 seats: Democrats take North Carolina and Maine, lose Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Kansas, and hold Michigan narrowly or not at all.
flip_trigger: On the night: Ohio called for Husted, or Brown trailing with 80 percent counted; Ossoff under +5 when Georgia reports around 9 pm ET; Rogers ahead in Michigan with Wayne County mostly in. Any one of these moves the primary to the alternate.

label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
weakest_component: The seat count under the new maps. No district polling exists in most redrawn seats, so the raters' calls are the only read.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and every midterm since 1994 with the president under 45 percent approval flipped the House when the other party did not already hold it. Trump is at 37.8 approve, 59.8 disapprove across 16 polls since Oct 20 (retrieved). Democrats hold 214 and need 218. The nonpartisan generic ballot averages D+8.1 over 28 polls since Oct 20, D+7.9 among likely voters (retrieved). The chamber model, which reads the raters' ratings for every House seat and shares one 3-point national swing, puts the chance at 81 with a mean of 231 seats (retrieved from scripts/chambers.py). Markets price 93 to 94.5. The model's width comes from its national swing and the ratings' coarseness, and the historical record argues for more than 81. The markets ignore the live downside: a 3-to-4-point poll miss toward Republicans, which I put near 30 percent, still clears 218 most of the time at D+4.5, but not always. Redistricting moved 16 seats toward Republicans and the raters already have 5 of them flipping. 88.
biggest_unknown: The size and direction of the generic-ballot miss. The record since 1994 is 1 to 4 points with no fixed direction in a midterm.
counter_case: The polls overstate Democrats by 5 or more, as in 1980 and 1948 nationally and never yet in a midterm, and the new maps are worth more than the raters show. Then the vote lands near D+3 and Republicans keep 218 to 222.
alternate: Republicans hold the House at 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: Before the election: a final likely-voter generic average under D+5. On the night: Democrats failing to flip PA-07, PA-08 and NY-17 by 11 pm ET, or a Republican lead in the national House vote with the East Coast counted.
